title: Canyon Run
description: Canyon Run is an Expo React Native app for GPS route capture, map visualization, and elevation-aware run review.

systemDesign: Canyon Run splits capture, storage, and visualization responsibilities into separate modules. That separation makes it easier to evolve map UX without risking GPS capture reliability or data persistence behavior.
learned: This project reinforced mobile sensor-system design tradeoffs: collect enough points for useful maps, but aggressively guard performance and persistence so sessions are never lost.

deepDive.title: GPS sampling in Track.jsx
deepDive.body: Track.jsx requests foreground permission with Location.requestForegroundPermissionsAsync in a mount effect and then calls Location.watchPositionAsync with Accuracy.BestForNavigation, timeInterval 1000 and distanceInterval 1. The user then picks a recording interval (a number plus a unit toggle), and the watch callback is meant to downsample the 1 Hz stream to that interval. Each recorded point is {longitude, latitude, altitude, timestamp: Date.now()} appended to routeJson state. There is no background location task, so tracking only works while the app is in the foreground. The subscription handle is kept in a useRef and removed in stopTracking.

deepDive.title: Interval logic has a stale-closure bug and dead code
deepDive.body: The watch callback is created once inside startTracking, so it closes over the lastRecordedLocation state value from that render, which is always null. The `if (!lastRecordedLocation)` branch therefore runs on every update and the time or distance throttle in the else branch is likely never reached; in practice every 1 Hz fix is probably recorded. The unit state is named timeUnit with values 'm' and 's' and a comment saying 'm' is meters, but the code multiplies by 60000 for 'm', so it is really minutes. The 'distance-based' else branch is unreachable because timeUnit is only ever 'm' or 's'. The commit message for f38f792 claims tracking by time or distance, but only time is actually wired up.

deepDive.title: Distance math
deepDive.body: Track.jsx defines calculateDistance as a haversine function with Earth radius 6371e3 meters, returning meters. dataManager.js has a second, separate haversine inside convertToRequiredFormat using R = 3959 (miles). That second one is only applied between the first and last point, so distance_miles stored for a run is the straight-line start-to-end displacement, not the path length. The end.meters field is computed as (points.length - 1) * interval, which is only meaningful for distance-based sampling and is wrong for time-based sampling. Altitude.jsx likewise fakes the x axis as index * 10 meters, assuming the 10 m spacing of the sample CSV.

deepDive.title: Map rendering and point simplification
deepDive.body: Maps.jsx (SimplifiedMaps) draws the route with react-native-svg Path and Circle rather than a tile map; an early Leaflet attempt (e9d0d3a, 27022f7) was abandoned when the project moved to Expo. processedCoordinates filters out non-numeric lat/lon and, beyond 50 points, decimates by a fixed stride of ceil(n/50) while always keeping the first and last point. This is uniform subsampling, not Douglas-Peucker, so sharp turns can be lost. mapBounds computes min/max lat/lon with a 15 percent margin and a single uniform scale, and geoToScreen flips Y and applies zoom and pan about a center at 65 percent of height. Longitude and latitude share one scale with no cos(lat) correction, so shapes are slightly distorted away from the equator.

deepDive.title: Zoom, pan and hit testing
deepDive.body: Zoom is clamped between 0.5 and 15 and driven by a PanResponder that only activates on two-finger touches, using the distance between touches to compute a scale ratio. Panning is done through arrow buttons that move panX/panY by a step that grows with zoom, capped at 500, plus a reset button; commit 42b3028 introduced this. Route stroke width and marker size scale inversely with zoom within fixed bounds. Tapping selects the nearest simplified point within 30 px using brute-force Euclidean search and opens a modal with that point's data. A code smell: the empty-state early return comes before the useMemo and useCallback hooks, which breaks React's rules of hooks if runData changes between empty and populated.

deepDive.title: Elevation profile
deepDive.body: Altitude.jsx builds an SVG line chart from parseFloat(point.altitude) over a synthetic distance axis. Its elevationGain stat is simply maxAltitude minus minAltitude, not cumulative ascent, so it is really elevation range. Y scaling uses the min/max range with a fallback height of 100 if flat, and grid lines are generated at distance steps of at least 100 with rounding. Altitude comes straight from the GPS altitude field with no smoothing or barometer data, so noisy values are plotted raw. Like Maps.jsx, it returns early before its useMemo hook.

deepDive.title: Persistence via a user-chosen JSON file
deepDive.body: The final app does not use the server. dataManager.js keeps a module-level CURRENT_FILE_PATH and reads and writes a whole JSON object of runs keyed by random id using expo-file-system. createNewRunsFile writes canyon_runs_YYYY-MM-DD.json to documentDirectory and offers it through expo-sharing; loadRunsFromFile uses expo-document-picker, copies the file to the app's writable directory and parses it. saveRun, updateRunLocation and deleteRun each do a full read-modify-write of the file, which is simple but not atomic or concurrency safe. Because the path is held in memory only, it is lost on app restart and the user must reload a file via FileManager.jsx each launch.

deepDive.title: Data format and CSV import tool
deepDive.body: Runs are stored as {id: {location, distance_miles, start, end, coordinates[]}}. This format came from an earlier iteration (ec45196, 7df53a3) and from client/assets/convertJson.js, a Node readline script that converts a CSV of lat, lon, meters, altitude columns (10_MetersCSV.csv, 10 m spacing) into that JSON with a random hex id. The CSV tool stores values as strings and null time, while the in-app saveRun stores numeric coordinates with timestamps, so the two producers disagree on types. Altitude.jsx copes with strings via parseFloat, but Maps.jsx filters strictly on typeof number, so CSV-converted canyons would likely be dropped from the map. There is no schema validation beyond typeof object on load.

deepDive.title: App state and navigation
deepDive.body: State is plain React useState with props drilling and no store. App.jsx toggles between FileManager and ViewSelector via a fileReady flag and passes savedRuns down. ViewSelector.jsx switches between tracker, map and elevation views, and Track.jsx raises onRunSelect and onRunsUpdate callbacks to the parent. Styling is centralized in components/shared/theme.js (added in 70ec04e). The UI is pure React Native with react-native-gesture-handler installed but the zoom actually relies on PanResponder.

deepDive.title: Abandoned backend and auth
deepDive.body: The server directory has an Express and Mongoose app (server.js) with a single POST /add-run taking name, latitude and longitude, and server-login.js with bcryptjs and jsonwebtoken login and register routes. Both listen on port 3000 and read the Mongo URI from environment variables, with a CORS allow list of localhost:4000, and server-login.js falls back to a hard-coded default JWT secret if JWT_SECRET is unset. Neither is called by the current client: client/components/api/db.js and authorization.js are leftovers, and Login.jsx and Register.jsx are not wired into App.jsx. The two server files duplicate each other, use different env variable names (MONGODB_URI vs URI), and the run schema does not match the app's run format. Treat the backend as an unfinished prototype.

architecture.summary: Offline-first Expo/React Native app. A foreground GPS watcher in Track.jsx produces timestamped points, dataManager.js persists them to a user-chosen JSON file, and Maps.jsx and Altitude.jsx render that data as SVG. An Express/Mongo backend and a CSV converter exist in the repo but are not part of the live data path.

deepDive.title: Client-only architecture on Expo Router and Firebase
deepDive.body: Insert is an Expo 54-era React Native app (package.json now pins expo ^58 and react-native 0.88) with expo-router as entry (app/_layout.tsx, app/index.tsx) and no backend server of its own. All persistence goes straight from the client to Firebase Auth, Firestore and Storage via the SDK, with security enforced only by firestore.rules. Navigation files exist (navigation/AppNavigators.tsx, AuthNavigators.tsx, RootNavigators.tsx), but the working app is driven by a very large app/index.tsx (about 40 KB) that switches screens with local state; the git log shows 'Add auth gating and simple screen navigation' and a later 'kitchen switcher & refactor tab/navigation'. Several screens are 50-76 KB single files (HomeScreen, RecipeListScreen, SocialScreen, RecipeFormScreen), so the structure is functional but monolithic.

deepDive.title: Firebase initialisation and session persistence
deepDive.body: screens/firebaseAuthLoginRegister/firebase/config.ts builds the app with getApps().length ? getApp() : initializeApp(...), then creates Auth through initializeAuth(app, { persistence: getReactNativePersistence(AsyncStorage) }). initializeAuth throws if Auth already exists (Fast Refresh), so createAuth() catches and falls back to getAuth(app). getReactNativePersistence is missing from the shared type declarations, so the import carries a @ts-expect-error. The firebaseConfig object is committed empty, so a cloner must fill in their own values (README step 2), and Firestore uses the full SDK rather than firebase/firestore/lite.

deepDive.title: Auth service and session revalidation
deepDive.body: authService.ts wraps Firebase email/password auth: normalizeEmail, isValidEmail, MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH = 8, signIn, register (which sends a verification email on a best-effort basis), resendVerificationEmail, requestPasswordReset and logout. requestPasswordReset swallows auth/user-not-found so the UI never reveals whether an account exists. getAuthErrorMessage maps Firebase error codes per context (login, register, reset). revalidateSession() calls user.reload() and getIdToken(true) and signs the user out only when the error code is in SESSION_INVALID_CODES (for example auth/user-not-found, auth/invalid-user-token); network errors are ignored so offline users stay signed in. UserDataProvider.tsx adds a shared context for user data.

deepDive.title: Firestore data model and security rules
deepDive.body: Data is per-user under users/{uid}/ with subcollections pantry, pendingPantry, recipes, shoppingList, settings, cookHistory, friends, friendRequests, outgoingFriendRequests, recipeShares and notifications (listed in accountDeletion.ts); global collections include socialPosts (with a comments subcollection), publicRecipes and a shared products collection keyed by barcode. firestore.rules gives owners read/write on their own subcollections, but excludes 'settings' from the broad rule because rules are additive. Cross-user writes are narrow: friend requests require fromUserId == auth.uid and status 'pending'; notifications are limited to type 'recipe_saved' with read == false; any signed-in user may update a post only if changedKeys().hasOnly(['likes']). Profiles forbid clients from setting or changing isAdmin. tests/firestore.rules.test.js runs these rules in the emulator through @firebase/rules-unit-testing via 'npm run test:rules'.

deepDive.title: Recipe import by scraping JSON-LD
deepDive.body: screens/utils/recipeImport.ts fetches a user-supplied http(s) URL directly from the device with a mobile Safari User-Agent, then uses regexes to pull every application/ld+json script block and og:image/twitter:image meta tags. findAllRecipeNodes walks the parsed JSON (including graphs) for schema.org Recipe nodes, and buildParsedRecipe converts them to ParsedRecipe with ingredients, instructions, servings, cookTime and up to 12 deduplicated imageCandidates. parseIngredient strips list prefixes, parentheticals and phrases like 'to taste', converts unicode fractions via a FRACTION_MAP, prefers metric values in parentheses, and normalises units through UNIT_NORMALIZE. splitInstructionText handles numbered steps and sentence splitting with dedupe. It is regex-based rather than a real HTML parser and relies on client-side fetch, so sites that block or do not expose JSON-LD fail with a user-facing error message.

deepDive.title: Ingredient matching and pantry availability
deepDive.body: screens/components/utils/ingredientUtils.ts holds a hand-written INGREDIENT_VARIANTS table (for example milk -> whole milk, 2% milk) and getBaseIngredient, and matchIngredient returns 'exact', 'base' or 'none'. checkRecipeAvailability sorts recipe ingredients into available, missing and partialMatches, and the useRecipeAvailability hook memoises this and computes canMakeRecipe (no missing) and a rounded percentageAvailable. Coverage is limited to the roughly 50 ingredients listed, so unusual ingredients always count as an exact string match or a miss. pantryDefault.ts and example data.json/recipes.json supply seed content.

deepDive.title: Allergy and dietary safety logic
deepDive.body: screens/utils/allergyMatching.ts defines ALLERGY_FAMILY_MAP, expanding allergens such as fish, shellfish, nut, peanut, dairy, egg, soy, sesame, wheat and gluten into member ingredient terms. normalizeText lowercases and strips punctuation, and withSimpleVariants generates plural and singular forms (including y -> ies) before matching. dietaryConflicts.ts has DIETARY_CONFLICT_KEYWORDS and getDietaryConflicts(ingredientNames, restrictions) for diets, and the recipe list uses both to filter. This is keyword matching, so it is a convenience heuristic and not medical-grade; hidden ingredients in compound products are not detected.

deepDive.title: Local state, offline helpers and unit handling
deepDive.body: State is React hooks and context (AuthContext, ThemeContext, usePantry, useRecipes) plus Firestore onSnapshot listeners; there is no Redux or caching layer. AsyncStorage is used for deleted example pantry item IDs (deletedExampleItemIds, added so seed items do not reappear), and the auth session. unitUtils.ts provides PreferredWeightUnit ('g' | 'lb') and UnitDisplayMode ('converted' | 'as_is') through formatQuantityForPreference. nutritionUtils.ts, locationUtils.ts and categorization.ts (RecipeBrowseCategory: breakfast, lunch, dinner, snack, dessert) support display and filtering. firebaseStorageUpload.ts uploads local files to Firebase Storage for recipe and step photos.

deepDive.title: Account deletion and data cleanup
deepDive.body: screens/utils/accountDeletion.ts deletes a user's data client-side in batches: deleteCollectionByPath loops with limit(300) and writeBatch, deletePublicRecipesOwnedByUser queries ownerId in pages of 150, and deleteSocialPostsOwnedByUser removes each post's comments first (pages of 80). removeReciprocalFriendLinks deletes the mirrored users/{friend}/friends/{uid} doc for each friend, with errors swallowed per doc. Because it is client-driven rather than a Cloud Function, an interrupted run can leave partial data, and it depends on the rules allowing those deletes. scripts/cleanup-legacy-quick-switch.js is a one-off migration for the retired admin quick-switch documents.

systemDesign: The project uses a simple embedded event loop: capture button input, update the virtual pet state, and reflect that state on the OLED with sound cues. That keeps the logic predictable and easy to debug on hardware.
learned: I learned how hardware constraints shape software design, especially when you need fast, understandable feedback from a very small interface.

deepDive.title: Cooperative super-loop with a state machine
deepDive.body: src/main.cpp runs everything from Arduino loop() with no RTOS tasks: it samples millis() once per pass, reads three debounced buttons and the obstacle sensor, services the buzzer, runs cheat-code matching, autosaves, then branches on a GameState enum (setup, egg, idle, sleeping, minigame show/input, game over). Each state returns early or falls through to stat decay, brain updates and rendering, and drawing is throttled to FRAME_INTERVAL (90 ms) so the I2C OLED is not flooded. All timers are stored as absolute millis timestamps and compared with unsigned subtraction (nowMs - lastX >= interval), which is wrap-safe for the 49-day millis rollover.

deepDive.title: Debounce and input handling
deepDive.body: Buttons A/B/C on GPIO23/18/19 use INPUT_PULLUP and a ButtonState struct processed by consumePress(), requiring a 30 ms (DEBOUNCE_MS) stable level before a press edge is reported once. The obstacle sensor on GPIO4 reuses the same idea in consumeObstacleDetected(): it tracks lastReadingDetected and lastEdgeMs, only promotes a reading to stableDetected after DEBOUNCE_MS, and reports only the rising edge. handleObstacleAlert adds a 1200 ms cooldown and branches by state: it wakes a sleeping pet, gives an idle pet +1 happiness and -1 anger through markCareAction, and does nothing in setup, egg or game over.

deepDive.title: Stat model and decay
deepDive.body: Hunger, happiness, energy and anger are integers clamped to 0..10 by clampStat. Each decays on its own base interval (90 s, 120 s, 150 s, and a 70 s anger cooldown), passed through adjustedInterval() which asks the brain for a trait-scaled interval via brainAdjustedInterval. During quiet hours the decay is slowed by QUIET_DECAY_MULTIPLIER (6x). Game over triggers when anger or hunger hits 10 or happiness or energy hits 0 in updateGameOver. The UI inverts hunger and anger into satisfaction-style bars so fuller is always better.

deepDive.title: Virtual clock and quiet hours
deepDive.body: There is no RTC or network time. The user sets the current hour, bedtime and wake hour in a first-boot setup screen, and virtualHour() computes (currentHourAtStart + (nowMs - clockEpochMs)/HOUR_MS) mod 24. inQuietHours handles both same-day windows and windows that wrap midnight (bedtime greater than wake), and returns false when they are equal. virtualDay() drives the day index used to reset dailyPlayCount. One weakness: clockEpochMs is persisted as a raw millis value under 'clkEp', but millis() restarts at zero on every boot, so after a power cycle (nowMs - clockEpochMs) appears to underflow as an unsigned long and the virtual hour and day can jump. The code never rebases that epoch on load.

deepDive.title: Adaptive personality brain
deepDive.body: src/pet_brain.cpp keeps eight traits (clingy, independent, energetic, lazy, irritable, cheerful, sensitive, stoic) as int16 scores clamped to -100..100 inside a PetBrain struct. Events like PET_EVENT_FEED_LATE or PLAY_WIN nudge traits by +/-1 in brainLearnFromEvent, a slow observer (every 4 s) learns from sustained patterns in learnFromPattern, and every 20 minutes decayTraitsTowardNeutral pulls each score one step toward zero so the personality can change. Traits feed back into gameplay: updateTalkDelay computes speech cooldown as 52 s minus clingy*120 ms plus independent*90 ms plus irritable*180 ms minus cheerful*45 ms, floored at 18 s, and brainAdjustedInterval scales decay. Dialogue prioritizes need-based lines, with rare optional chatter scheduled 15 to 30 minutes ahead using esp_random().

deepDive.title: Adaptive sequence mini-game
deepDive.body: The mini-game shows a pattern of buttons 1..3 (up to MAX_PATTERN_LEN 20) with 650 ms steps and a 4.5 s input timeout. minigameTargetLength starts at 4 and adds dailyPlayCount/2, capped by a learned memoryCeiling (default 13, floor 4). When the desired length exceeds the ceiling it occasionally (35 percent) tries one step above to probe for improvement. updateMemoryCeilingFromResult raises the ceiling after 3 near-cap wins in a row and lowers it after 3 cap-level failures, and persists the value to NVS under 'memCap'.

deepDive.title: Persistence across power loss
deepDive.body: saveGameState writes about 40 short-keyed values into the ESP32 Preferences namespace 'petcfg' every 5 seconds (AUTOSAVE_INTERVAL_MS): state, species, stats, brain traits (versioned with 'pVer'), mood and popup text, schedule, difficulty memory and the mini-game pattern serialized as a digit string. Timers are saved as elapsed deltas via elapsedSince and rebuilt after boot with restoreTimestamp(nowMs, elapsed), so they survive the millis() reset. loadGameState clamps stats and the hatch duration and falls back to idle if the state byte is out of range. A cheat sequence 'ABCCABBACABC' calls preferences.clear() and resets runtime state. Writing that many NVS keys every 5 s is aggressive for flash wear and is not rate-limited when nothing changed.

deepDive.title: Rendering and audio
deepDive.body: An Adafruit SSD1306 128x64 display on I2C (SDA 21, SCL 22, address 0x3C) draws 16x16 bitmap sprites from src/pet_assets.cpp for the egg (normal and cracked) and four species (Dino, Dog, Cat, Alien) with an alternate animation frame. Faces and eyes are drawn procedurally in drawFace and drawEyePair, speech is word-wrapped into three 16-character lines by wrapText, and status text scrolls in 21-character windows. The active buzzer on GPIO15 uses ledcSetup/ledcWriteTone on channel 0 at 2200 Hz and pulses 40 ms on and 140 ms off while a speech popup is visible, and is muted entirely while the obstacle sensor is active.

title: OrderInventory
description: Company-scoped inventory app that imports Excel workbooks, routes edits through admin approval, and keeps versioned audit history.
overview: OrderInventory is one Expo Router codebase targeting Android, iOS and web. Members import messy Excel sheets, which are normalized client-side, then published or submitted for admin approval through Firebase Cloud Functions backed by Firestore with security rules.
highlights: Excel parser maps arbitrary headers to canonical fields using an alias table with exact match first, then substring fuzzy match
Unmapped columns are preserved as customFields so no spreadsheet data is lost
Join codes are 12 chars from an unambiguous alphabet via crypto.randomBytes, stored only as SHA-256 hashes, and expire after 60 seconds
All writes go through callable Cloud Functions with company-admin checks, plus Firestore rules, audit logging and immutable inventory snapshots
demoDescription: The core workflow turns an arbitrary spreadsheet into validated inventory rows and moves them through an approval pipeline.
demoBullets: Upload an .xlsx file and see headers auto-mapped to item code, name, quantity, unit, location and status
Members submit changes for approval while admins review and approve or reject
Admins generate short-lived join codes to add teammates to a company
Browse earlier inventory snapshots and export the current inventory back to Excel

systemDesign: A thin Expo client does Excel parsing locally and calls callable Cloud Functions for every protected read and write. Functions use the Admin SDK, check company roles, write audit records and versioned snapshots to Firestore, and a scheduled function deletes expired join-code hashes. Firestore security rules add a second authorization layer.
learned: I learned to keep trust on the server: the client only parses and displays, while Cloud Functions and Firestore rules decide what is allowed. Building the header matcher taught me how forgiving spreadsheet import has to be, and that fuzzy matching needs an exact-match pass first to avoid wrong mappings. Hashing short-lived join codes was my first practical use of storing only a digest of a secret.

deepDive.title: Server-mediated multi-tenant model
deepDive.body: Every tenant is a companies/{companyId} document with a memberships/{userId} subcollection holding role ('admin' or 'member') and status ('active' or 'removed'). Nearly all state changes go through 2nd-gen Cloud Functions callables (functions/src/index.js re-exports about 18 of them) rather than direct client writes. Shared helpers in functions/src/admin.js (requireAuth, requireCompanyAdmin, requireCompanyMember) re-read the membership document with the Admin SDK on every call, so authorization never trusts client-supplied roles or a cached token claim. The client wrappers in services/companyService.js and services/inventoryService.js are thin httpsCallable calls that map a 'not-found' error to a hint to deploy functions.

deepDive.title: Join-code hashing, TTL and cleanup
deepDive.body: joinCodes.js builds a 12-character invite code from crypto.randomBytes(12) mapped onto a 32-character alphabet that drops look-alike characters (no I, O, 0, 1). Only a SHA-256 hash (codeHash) and a 4-character codePrefix are stored, and the raw code is returned once to the admin. Codes live for 60 seconds (JOIN_CODE_TTL_MS). validateJoinCodeServer uppercases and trims the input, hashes it, queries joinCodes by codeHash plus status 'active', and if the code is past expiresAt it deletes the document and logs a failed joinAttempt. On success a single batch creates the member membership, merges the user profile, and increments useCount. Codes are not single-use: useCount is only incremented, so any number of people can join within the 60 second window. A scheduled function, deleteExpiredJoinCodes, runs every minute and deletes up to 500 expired hashes. Note that companies.js carries its own copy of createJoinCode and hashJoinCode, and that copy does not trim or uppercase before hashing.

deepDive.title: Firestore security rules as a second wall
deepDive.body: firestore.rules ends in a default-deny match on /{document=**}, and joinCodes, auditLogs, inventoryImports, submissions and memberships are all closed to client writes (join codes are closed to reads as well). Users can create their own profile only with a whitelisted key set, and updates are limited via diff().affectedKeys().hasOnly([...]) while role and companyId must be unchanged, which blocks self-promotion. Company membership checks use exists()/get() on the membership path, so rules and functions share the same source of truth. inventoryItems allow member reads and writes only where lastEditedBy == request.auth.uid and lastEditedAt == request.time, which forces server-stamped audit fields, and deletes are denied. The inventoryVersions and inventoryApprovals collections have no explicit rule, so default deny means only functions touch them.

deepDive.title: Excel import pipeline
deepDive.body: services/excelParser.js uses SheetJS (xlsx) to read the first worksheet from a File, Blob, URI, ArrayBuffer or typed array. It converts the sheet to a matrix, finds the first non-empty row as the header, and maps each header to one of eight canonical fields (itemCode, name, description, category, quantity, unit, location, status) through HEADER_ALIASES, using an exact alias match first and a fuzzy substring match second. Unrecognized headers become dynamic columns with field 'customFields.<camelCase>', and their values are stored in row.customFields. Fallbacks are explicit: a missing itemCode becomes the first non-empty cell or 'ROW-n', quantity defaults to 1 (or reads a company-configured quantityColumnName), and location falls back to the company's defaultLocation. Quantity is coerced with Number() and throws on non-finite values. The fuzzy match is loose: the 'description' alias also appears under name, and any short header that is a substring of an alias can match.

deepDive.title: Approval workflow and immutable versions
deepDive.body: Members cannot publish. submitInventoryForApprovalServer writes a pending document to inventoryApprovals containing the submitted rows and sanitized columns. Admins call getPendingInventoryApprovalsServer, which diffs each submission against the live inventoryItems for the company and returns added, removed and edited changes. reviewInventoryApprovalServer then runs one batch: on approval it upserts each row under the deterministic id '{companyId}_{encodeURIComponent(itemCode)}' with merge, updates the company's inventoryColumns, and creates an inventoryVersions snapshot with source 'memberApproval'. Admin direct publishes in saveInventoryServer produce the same snapshot with source 'adminPublish'. Item ids derived from companyId plus itemCode make re-imports idempotent but also mean a row whose itemCode changes becomes a different document.

deepDive.title: Version diffing algorithm
deepDive.body: inventoryVersions.js compareVersions indexes both row lists in a Map keyed by rowKey (itemCode, else id, else 'row-index'), then emits 'added' for keys only in the new set, 'removed' for keys only in the old set, and 'edited' when getChangedFields finds differences. getChangedFields flattens nested objects to dot paths with flattenRow, skipping bookkeeping keys such as createdAt and lastEditedBy, compares via JSON.stringify, caps results at 20 fields, and prettifies labels with formatFieldLabel. getInventoryVersionsServer sorts snapshots in memory by createdAt, keeps the newest 50, diffs each against the next older one, marks the oldest as a baseline, and strips the heavy rows array from the response. It resolves creator, submitter and reviewer names through adminAuth.getUser per version, which is an N+1 lookup pattern.

deepDive.title: Audit logging with an allow-list and redaction
deepDive.body: audit.js exposes secureAuditLogWrite, the only path that writes auditLogs. It rejects any action not in VALID_ACTIONS (a few names are listed twice, which is harmless), checks that the actor is an active member of the claimed company, and snapshots actor email and name from Firebase Auth. sanitizeMetadata drops any key matching password, token, secret, rawcode, codehash or authorization, keeps only string, number and boolean values, and truncates strings to 500 characters. getAuditHistoryServer is admin-only, filters out noisy inventory-change actions and the join-code generate/revoke events (HIDDEN_AUDIT_ACTIONS), sorts newest first and returns 200 events. Because the client can call writeAuditEventServer with any allowed action name, 'client activity' entries such as open or download are self-reported and not tamper-proof.

deepDive.title: Client app, roles and barcode scanning
deepDive.body: A single Expo Router codebase (SDK 57, React 19, React Native 0.86, NativeWind) targets iOS, Android and web, with Firebase Hosting serving the web export from dist with an SPA rewrite. src/components/role-guard.tsx reads users/{uid} through getUserAccess and redirects unless the role matches (admins pass member guards), which is a UX gate backed by the real checks in functions and rules. src/app/inventory.tsx is by far the largest screen (about 43 KB) and mixes edit mode, import, export, submission and an expo-camera CameraView barcode scanner. A scan becomes the itemCode and the app requires any company-defined requiredColumnFields to be filled before the new row can be added. Barcode scanning is feature-flagged by the company's allowBarcodeScanning setting, which updateCompanySettingsServer validates, trims and length-caps field by field.

deepDive.title: Unfinished and rough edges
deepDive.body: functions/src/email.js is a placeholder: sendInventoryEmail validates input and writes an audit record but returns provider 'placeholder' and never sends mail. Several callables in inventoryVersions.js throw plain Error objects instead of HttpsError, so callers receive a generic internal error rather than a precise permission-denied or invalid-argument status; requireAuth in admin.js has the same problem. Debug console.log lines remain in the save and submit paths, and a 166 KB firebase-debug.log is committed to the repository. getPendingInventoryApprovalsServer loads the entire company inventory to diff against, which will not scale to large catalogs, and Firestore documents holding full rows arrays are bounded by the 1 MiB document limit.

Firestore rules deny almost all direct client writes, so functions are the sole writer for memberships, join codes, audit logs, approvals and versions.

title: Sproutie
description: Plant care app with an Express and MongoDB backend that wraps the Trefle plant API and stores each user's plant collection.
overview: Sproutie is a React Native/Expo plant-care app paired with a Node.js/Express server. Users authenticate with Firebase, search plant species through the server, and save plants to a personal collection with growth stages, notes and care reminders. Weather-based watering notifications are described in the README as a goal.
highlights: Duplicate-save guard looks up the compound key (firebaseUid, trefleId) and returns HTTP 409 instead of inserting twice
Mongoose compound indexes, including a unique (firebaseUid, trefleId) index on favorites, keep per-user lookups fast
TrefleAPI service class wraps the third-party API, appends the token correctly with ? or &, and URL-encodes search queries
Schema models care reminders (type, frequency, lastDone, nextDue) and growth stages per plant
demoDescription: The server exposes REST endpoints that the app uses to find plants and manage a personal collection.
demoBullets: Search species with GET /api/plants/search?q=
Save a plant to a user's collection with POST /api/plants/save
List a user's plants newest first and remove entries by id
Create the Mongo user record right after Firebase registration

diagramSteps.title: Authenticate
diagramSteps.detail: Firebase handles sign-in; the app posts the Firebase UID and email to /api/users to create the Mongo profile.

diagramSteps.title: Search
diagramSteps.detail: The app calls the server, which proxies Trefle with the API token kept in an environment variable.

diagramSteps.detail: The save route checks required fields and rejects duplicates by (firebaseUid, trefleId).

systemDesign: A React Native client talks to an Express REST API split into routes, models and a service layer. Mongoose models hold users, saved plants, favorites and search history with compound indexes on the Firebase UID. The server hides the Trefle API token from the client. Note that the user id is taken from the request body, so server-side token verification is not yet implemented.
learned: I learned to separate routes, models and an external-API service class, and to use compound indexes and 409 responses to keep saves idempotent. Reading my own code back, I also see that trusting a userId from the request body is a gap; the next step is verifying Firebase ID tokens on the server.

deepDive.title: Two-package layout: Expo app plus Express API
deepDive.body: The repo holds two separate Node projects: sproutie/ (an Expo Router React Native app, with screens under app/) and server/ (an Express 4 + Mongoose 8 API). The two talk over plain fetch to a base URL read from EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL. Both apiService.ts and server.js fall back to a hardcoded LAN address (192.168.0.17:3000), so the app only works against a dev machine on that network unless the env var is set. There is no deployment config, Dockerfile, or CI in the repo; it is a local-dev project.

deepDive.title: Authentication: Firebase on the client, UID as the only identity on the server
deepDive.body: Login and registration use the Firebase Web SDK (firebase/auth) through app/firebase/auth.ts (signUp, signIn, logOut, subscribeToAuthChanges) and the login/ and register/ screens, with sendPasswordResetEmail on login. app/index.tsx conditionally renders Login, Register, or HomeScreen based on auth state. The Express server never verifies a Firebase ID token: routes trust a firebaseUid or userId sent in the URL or JSON body. Any caller who knows a UID can read, save, or delete that user's plants, so this is not real authorization yet. Commit 8b62fe7 cites a JWT tutorial in its message, but no JWT or token verification code exists.

deepDive.title: MongoDB data model and indexes
deepDive.body: server/models/User.js defines a User with a unique, indexed firebaseUid, lowercase email, displayName, emailVerified, isActive, and timestamps. It has a pre('save') hook that bumps updatedAt and a static findByFirebaseUid that filters isActive: true. server/models/Plant.js defines three Mongoose models: UserPlant, FavoritePlant, and PlantSearch. UserPlant mirrors Trefle fields (trefleId, slug, scientificName, family, genus, imageUrl, synonyms and so on) and adds user fields such as nickname, notes, plantedDate, photos[], growthStages[], and careReminders[]. It has compound indexes on {firebaseUid, isActive}, {trefleId}, and {firebaseUid, trefleId}. FavoritePlant has a unique {firebaseUid, trefleId} index and PlantSearch has {firebaseUid, searchDate: -1}. Only UserPlant is used by any route; FavoritePlant, PlantSearch, and most growth and care fields are schema only.

deepDive.title: REST API surface
deepDive.body: server.js mounts /api/users and /api/plants, plus /health (reports mongoose.connection.readyState) and a root endpoint listing endpoints. routes/users.js has POST / (validates firebaseUid and email, checks for an existing user, and maps Mongo duplicate-key code 11000 to a 400) and GET /:firebaseUid (404 if absent). routes/plants.js has GET / (Trefle plant list), GET /search?q=, POST /save, DELETE /delete/:plantId, and GET /user/:userId (sorted by createdAt desc). A global error middleware returns a 500 JSON body. cors() is wide open and there is no rate limiting, validation library, or pagination.

deepDive.title: Trefle API wrapper and save/dedupe logic
deepDive.body: server/services/trefleAPI.js is a small class that reads TREFLE_API_TOKEN (throwing in the constructor if missing) and has a private _fetch that appends the token as a query parameter with node-fetch. It exposes getPlants() and searchPlants(query) with encodeURIComponent. It has no timeout, retry, status-code check, or caching, and it returns response.json() even on upstream errors. The separate server/config/trefle.js declares baseURL, timeout and a 120 requests/minute rateLimit but reads a different variable (TREFLE_API_KEY) and is not imported anywhere. POST /api/plants/save maps Trefle snake_case fields to the camelCase schema and does a findOne on {firebaseUid, trefleId} first, returning 409 with the existing plant; this is a check-then-insert race, because the UserPlant compound index is not unique.

deepDive.title: Search and collection screen
deepDive.body: app/screens/plants/searchPlants/index.jsx holds the main user feature. It has an apiCall wrapper that throws on non-OK responses, a searchPlants flow against /api/plants/search, and a collection list loaded from /api/plants/user/:userId. It also keeps a Set of saved Trefle IDs (savedPlantIds) so the UI can detect duplicates without scanning arrays. The user id comes from getCurrentUser in firebase/auth.ts. Save and remove call the POST and DELETE routes; commit 58d2126 changed removal from POST /remove to DELETE /delete/:plantId, with userId still sent in the DELETE body. Errors surface as alert() popups rather than structured UI state. The separate screens/plants/index.jsx is a simpler 'Show Plants' button that lists the raw Trefle plant list.

deepDive.title: Navigation and screen state
deepDive.body: screens/home/index.jsx implements a hand-rolled bottom tab bar using useState('plants' | 'search' | 'profile') and a switch statement, rather than Expo Router tabs. Despite the tab-bar commit, there is no global state store; auth state is subscribed to in app/index.tsx and each screen fetches its own data. The tab icons are emoji, and the source file shows mojibake in them (likely an encoding mishap). PlantCard.jsx and plants/styles.ts are stubs added late in the history and are not wired in.

deepDive.title: Location service (built, not yet integrated with weather)
deepDive.body: services/locationService.ts wraps expo-location with requestLocationPermission (foreground only), getCurrentLocation (Accuracy.Balanced, returns null if denied), and getAddressFromCoords (reverseGeocodeAsync). Each function catches errors, logs them, and returns false or null. components/requests/location.jsx drives it with loading, approved, location, and address state and shows Alert dialogs for granted, denied, and error cases, reading the city from the first reverse-geocode result. The UI copy promises weather-based care recommendations, but no weather API, no notification code, and no backend location fields exist. Tasks.txt lists weather service, storing location in the User model, and weather alerts as upcoming work.

deepDive.title: Profile screen, config hygiene, and unfinished pieces
deepDive.body: ProfileScreen is incomplete: it declares const userInfo = null and then assigns to it in fetchUserData (which would throw), takes UID as a component prop (React passes props), is never called, and renders 'Coming Soon...'. server/config/database.js is an unused standalone MongoClient ping script that logs the full connection URI, which risks leaking credentials in logs; the real connection is mongoose.connect in server.js, which exits the process on failure. server/sproutMongoDbScript.js is a zero-byte file. The Firebase web config is committed in app/firebase/config.ts (normal for web keys), and .env files are gitignored. Tasks.txt is a long roadmap and the README documents setup; there are no tests.

Location access uses the device through expo-location but is not yet connected to any backend or weather source.

title: Spotify Friend
description: React Native prototype exploring Spotify's PKCE authorization flow, with a planned song play-count tracker.
overview: The repo contains an Expo React Native App.js with TODOs for tallying song plays in a dictionary, and an assets/script.js that implements pieces of the Spotify Authorization Code with PKCE flow: verifier generation, SHA-256 challenge, token exchange and profile fetch. It is unfinished and not wired together.
highlights: PKCE code verifier built from 128 random characters
S256 code challenge using SHA-256 and base64url encoding (replace + and /, strip =)
Token exchange posts authorization code plus verifier to the Spotify token endpoint
Planned song-count dictionary; the auth flow is incomplete and the app does not run end to end
demoDescription: A prototype of the Spotify login steps; the UI is not finished.
demoBullets: Generates verifier and challenge for PKCE
Exchanges code for an access token
Fetches the profile from /v1/me
Song play counting is still TODO

diagramSteps.title: Verifier
diagramSteps.detail: Generate a random 128 character string and keep it in local storage.

diagramSteps.title: Challenge
diagramSteps.detail: SHA-256 hash the verifier and base64url encode it.

diagramSteps.title: Authorize
diagramSteps.detail: Redirect to Spotify with the S256 challenge (the redirect line is commented out).

diagramSteps.title: Token
diagramSteps.detail: Exchange the returned code and verifier for an access token, then call /v1/me.

systemDesign: A React Native App.js shell plus a script module holding the OAuth helper functions. The pieces are not yet connected, and the script mixes Node-style crypto with a mobile client, which I would need to fix.
learned: I learned how PKCE protects the authorization code flow without a client secret. The code also shows my limits: it uses Math.random for the verifier and Node modules in a mobile app, so I would switch to a secure random source and an Expo-compatible crypto library next.

deepDive.title: What this repo actually is
deepDive.body: spotifyFriend is an early-stage Expo (SDK 51, React Native 0.74) scaffold meant to show Spotify listening data, such as how many times each song was played. Only about two commits exist, and the UI layer is unfinished: App.js declares a user state and an empty songs dictionary, and renders a FlatList whose data prop references userData, a variable that is never defined, so the app would not run as committed. The README is a title only. Honest summary: this is a learning prototype where the OAuth plumbing was started and left incomplete.

deepDive.title: PKCE authorization flow in assets/script.js
deepDive.body: The script follows Spotify's Authorization Code with PKCE tutorial. generateCodeVerifier(128) builds a 128-character string from an alphanumeric alphabet using Math.random, which is not cryptographically secure (the PKCE spec recommends a CSPRNG). generateCodeChallenge hashes the verifier with Node crypto SHA-256 and base64url-encodes it by swapping + and / and stripping '=' padding, which is the correct S256 transform. redirectToAuthCodeFlow builds URLSearchParams with client_id, response_type=code, a localhost:5173 redirect URI, scope 'user-read-private user-read-email', code_challenge_method S256 and the challenge.

deepDive.title: Token exchange and profile fetch
deepDive.body: getAccessToken posts to https://accounts.spotify.com/api/token with grant_type=authorization_code, the code, redirect URI and stored code_verifier as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, then reads access_token from the JSON. fetchProfile calls the Web API /v1/me with a Bearer header, and populateUI is entirely commented-out browser DOM code. The scope list only covers profile and email; reading listening history would need scopes like user-read-recently-played or user-top-read, and none of those endpoints are called yet.

deepDive.title: Control-flow bugs left in place
deepDive.body: handleAuth checks 'if (code)' and then starts the redirect, which is inverted: the redirect should happen when no code is present. The else branch calls getAccessToken(clientId, code) with a clientId variable that is never declared, and the author left a '//!: Need to find out what clientID is' note about it. The authorization redirect itself is commented out because document.location does not exist in React Native or Node, and code is hard-coded to undefined. The file also calls handleAuth() at import time and logs 'working' and 'done', so it runs as a side effect when imported.

deepDive.title: Platform mismatch
deepDive.body: The PKCE code uses Node-only modules (crypto from npm and node-localstorage) that do not work inside a React Native bundle, and App.js imports handleAuth and friends from it. The verifier is persisted to a file under assets/scratch through node-localstorage, and that scratch file got committed. A working mobile version would use expo-auth-session or expo-crypto plus AsyncStorage/SecureStore with a custom-scheme redirect. This mismatch is the main reason the project stalled at this stage.

deepDive.title: Secrets hygiene
deepDive.body: A Spotify client identifier appears hard-coded in script.js and again in assets/CLIENT_CODE.env, which is committed, and the PKCE verifier file is committed too. A client ID is a public value in PKCE flows (no client secret is used, which is the right choice for a mobile app), but the committed verifier is a one-time secret that should never be tracked. The package.json also lists the deprecated 'crypto' npm placeholder package, which adds nothing over Node's built-in module.

title: Dino Game
description: A Chrome-style endless runner built with vanilla JavaScript and the HTML5 Canvas.
overview: A single-page canvas game where a dinosaur jumps over randomly spawned cacti. It uses a requestAnimationFrame loop, simple gravity physics, and AABB collision detection, all in one small script with no libraries.
highlights: requestAnimationFrame game loop that clears and redraws the canvas every frame
Gravity physics: velocityY += gravity each frame, with the dino clamped to the ground using Math.min
Axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) collision detection between the dino and each cactus
Weighted random cactus spawning (about 70% small, 20% medium, 10% large) on a 1 second interval, capped at 5 live obstacles
demoDescription: Run the game in a browser and jump over cacti until you collide with one.
demoBullets: Press Space or Arrow Up to jump
Jumping is only allowed while the dino is on the ground
Score increases every frame
On collision the sprite swaps to a dead dino and the loop stops

diagramSteps.title: Input
diagramSteps.detail: A keydown listener sets velocityY to -10 when the dino is on the ground.

diagramSteps.title: Update
diagramSteps.detail: Gravity is added to velocityY, dino.y is clamped at ground level, and cacti move left by velocityX.

diagramSteps.title: Collide
diagramSteps.detail: Each cactus is checked against the dino with an AABB overlap test.

diagramSteps.title: Render
diagramSteps.detail: The canvas is cleared and sprites plus the score are redrawn, then the next frame is requested.

systemDesign: Everything lives in one script with module-level state (dino and cactus objects, velocity, gravity, score, gameOver). A requestAnimationFrame loop drives updates and rendering, while a separate setInterval spawns obstacles. Spawned cacti are copied from a template object and stored in a small array that drops the oldest entry past five.
learned: I learned how a basic game loop works: update state, test collisions, then redraw. I got comfortable with simple gravity physics and AABB overlap checks. Looking back, the game speed is tied to frame rate and cactus spawning uses a fixed timer, so a fixed timestep and a spawn gap tied to speed would make it more consistent.

deepDive.title: Game loop and frame-coupled physics
deepDive.body: assets/script.js drives the game with requestAnimationFrame(update), re-registering itself at the top of every frame unless gameOver is set. Nothing uses a delta time: velocityX is a fixed -8 px per frame, gravity is 0.4 px per frame squared and score increments once per frame. That makes game speed proportional to the display refresh rate, so a 144 Hz monitor plays roughly 2.4x faster than a 60 Hz one. It is the most important limitation of the implementation.

deepDive.title: Jump arithmetic
deepDive.body: Each frame adds gravity to velocityY and sets dino.y = Math.min(dino.y + velocityY, 156), where 156 is the ground line (board height 250 minus sprite height 94) so the clamp doubles as the ground collision. moveDino only fires on Space or ArrowUp and only when dino.y equals exactly 156, which prevents double jumps; the strict float comparison works because Math.min lands exactly on 156. A jump sets velocityY to -10, giving an apex of about 10 * 25 / 2 = 125 px after roughly 25 frames and about 50 frames of airtime, close to 0.8 s at 60 fps.

deepDive.title: Obstacle spawning
deepDive.body: placeCactus runs on a separate setInterval(placeCactus, 1000), independent of the animation loop. One Math.random() draw selects the sprite and width: above 0.90 the 102 px triple cactus (10 percent), above 0.70 the 69 px double (20 percent), otherwise the 34 px single (70 percent). Each spawn pushes a shallow copy ({...cactus}) of a template object at x = 700, and the array is trimmed to five entries with shift(). Cacti are not removed when they leave the screen except by that cap, so off-screen cacti keep being moved and collision-tested until evicted.

deepDive.title: AABB collision
deepDive.body: detectCollision(a, b) is a standard axis-aligned bounding-box overlap test using four inequalities (a.x < b.x + b.width, a.x + a.width > b.x, and the same on y). It is applied to the full sprite rectangles, with no hitbox shrinking, so the 88x94 dino can register hits on transparent corners. On a hit, endGame sets gameOver, swaps dinoImg.src to dino-dead.png and redraws the sprite in its onload handler; the loop stops on the next frame, so the dead sprite is drawn once over the last frame.

deepDive.title: Bug history: shared object aliasing
deepDive.body: The first version of placeCactus mutated one global cactus template and pushed that same reference into cactusArray several times, so all obstacles shared an x position and sprite. Per commit ea6c3d6 it also used per-type width fields that were never defined on the object, and an empty branch skipped spawns when the random draw was 0.5 or below. The later refactor collapsed the branching into ternaries and pushes {...cactus}, which fixes the aliasing and removes the dead zone so every tick spawns a cactus.

deepDive.title: Unfinished parts
deepDive.body: The img folder ships assets that the code never uses: birds, ducking and running animation frames, clouds, a track, a reset button and a game-over banner. There is no restart: once gameOver is true the loop stops and the player must reload the page, and difficulty never scales since velocityX is constant. The score is drawn with fillText(++score, 5, 20) so it counts frames, not distance or time. The README in this repo describes the variables and functions well but is a flat list rather than design documentation.

title: React Weather
description: A React weather app that looks up a city and shows current conditions from OpenWeatherMap.
overview: Users type a city name and the app fetches current weather from the OpenWeatherMap API in imperial units, then shows an icon matching the condition plus temperature, min/max, humidity and wind. A 404 response shows a city-not-found error.
highlights: useEffect triggered by city state to fetch data from the REST API whenever a new city is submitted
Async fetch with HTTP 404 handling that clears stale data and sets an error flag
Lookup-table mapping of the API weather.main value to an icon image
Component split into Info, Card, Block, Menu and Navigation with CSS Modules styling
demoDescription: Enter a city name and submit to see its current weather.
demoBullets: Empty submissions trigger an alert asking for a city
Condition icon is chosen from the API response
Shows temperature, min, max, humidity and wind speed
Unknown cities display an error message

diagramSteps.detail: The form handler reads the input and sets the city state.

diagramSteps.title: Fetch
diagramSteps.detail: A useEffect on city calls the OpenWeatherMap current weather endpoint.

diagramSteps.detail: A 404 sets the error state; otherwise the JSON is stored in weatherData.

systemDesign: A Create React App client with no backend. The Info component owns three pieces of state (city, error, weatherData) and calls the public API directly from the browser. Weather icons are imported as a module and mapped by condition name. Styling uses CSS Modules.
learned: I learned the useState and useEffect data-fetching pattern and how to handle an error response from an API. Honestly, the API key is hardcoded in the client source, which I would now move to an environment variable or a proxy. The weathers array check also does nothing useful, and a network failure other than 404 is not handled.

deepDive.title: Component structure
deepDive.body: A Create React App project (react-scripts 5, React 18) whose tree is App -> Navigation + Card -> Info. Info.jsx owns all behavior: three useState hooks (city, error, weatherData), a fetch function, a submit handler and the render. Card.jsx wraps Info and prints the current date; Navigation.jsx is a static header with Menu and Theme placeholders. Block.jsx duplicates the weather display markup from Info as a presentational component taking weatherData and weatherComponents props, but nothing imports it, so the extraction was started and not finished.

deepDive.title: Data flow and API usage
deepDive.body: handleSubmit reads the city from e.target.elements[0].value (an uncontrolled input) and calls setCity. A useEffect keyed on [city] then runs fetchWeather, which calls the OpenWeatherMap current-weather endpoint (data/2.5/weather) with units=imperial and q=<city>. A 404 sets error=true and clears weatherData; any other status is parsed as JSON and shown. The input is not URL-encoded, and non-404 failures (401 bad key, 429 rate limit, network errors) are not handled, so they would parse an error body as if it were weather data and then crash on weatherData.weather[0].

deepDive.title: Rendering weather conditions
deepDive.body: The first element of data.weather (e.g. 'Clouds', 'Rain') is lowercased and used as a key into a weatherComponents object built from img/img.jsx, which re-exports ten PNG icons by name. A weathers array with an includes() check renders an empty fragment either way, which is leftover logic. OpenWeatherMap group names such as Thunderstorm, Fog or Haze have no entry, so for those conditions the img src would be undefined. Temperature, min/max, humidity and wind are shown as raw numbers without unit labels even though imperial units are requested.

deepDive.title: Date display bug
deepDive.body: Card.jsx maps month names in an object keyed 1 through 12 but indexes it with date.getMonth(), which is zero-based. As a result the month is off by one: January would render as undefined and December would show as November. This is a genuine defect that remains in the final commit.

deepDive.title: Security and configuration
deepDive.body: The OpenWeatherMap API key is hard-coded as a string constant inside Info.jsx and committed, and any browser-side key is visible in network requests anyway. The proper fix is to rotate the key and proxy the request through a small server or use a build-time environment variable with the understanding that it is still public to the client. package.json also lists a stray 'react-script' dependency next to react-scripts.

deepDive.title: Unfinished roadmap
deepDive.body: A Todo comment appended to public/index.html lists planned work: move the search input into the nav, add a plus button to save cities as cards, and add transitions. ASCII.jsx contains ASCII-art weather components that are not used (and whose emoji have been mangled by an encoding problem), and the Menu button and Theme entry have no behavior. The latest commit also pasted an AI-generated suggestion about splitting Info.jsx into WeatherAPI, WeatherForm and WeatherDisplay into public/index.html as text, which suggests a refactor was considered but never carried out. The README is a generic template with a placeholder clone URL.

title: geoToDo
description: A full-stack task manager with an Expo React Native client and an Express/MongoDB API, aimed at location-aware to-dos.
overview: The mobile app shows tasks in Today, Future and Locations tabs and lets tasks move between Open, WIP and Closed. The Node/Express server connects to MongoDB and serves task data over a REST API. The geolocation features are planned in the structure, but I did not find actual distance or geofence code in the files I read.
highlights: Two-part architecture: Expo Router app in toDo/ and Express API in server/
Controller-per-resource API layout (runs, tasks, users, locations) using Express routers
MongoDB access through the official driver with Stable API strict mode and env-based URI
Tabbed task views (Today, Future, Locations) with status filtering and PATCH-based status updates described in the README
demoDescription: Start the Express server with a MongoDB URI, then launch the Expo app.
demoBullets: Server needs MONGO_URI in a .env file
GET /api/runs returns documents from MongoDB
Expo app renders User and ToDo components from the index route
Client expects the server at localhost:3000

diagramSteps.title: App
diagramSteps.detail: Expo Router renders the User and ToDo components.

diagramSteps.title: Request
diagramSteps.detail: The client uses fetch against the Express API.

diagramSteps.detail: Express routes call the MongoDB driver and return JSON.

diagramSteps.detail: Task documents live in a MongoDB collection.

systemDesign: A separate client and server. The client uses file-based routing (Expo Router) with tab components per view. The server loads the MongoDB URI from the environment, enables CORS and JSON parsing, and organizes endpoints into controller files per resource. Currently only the runs route is clearly wired up in server.js.
learned: I learned how to connect an Expo client to an Express and MongoDB backend and keep secrets in environment variables. Honestly, the server opens and closes a MongoDB connection on every request, which is wasteful; a shared connection would be better. The location features are not implemented in the code I reviewed, so this is more of a CRUD foundation so far.

deepDive.title: Repository layout and current scope
deepDive.body: geoToDo is split into toDo/ (an Expo SDK 53 / React Native 0.79 app using expo-router) and server/ (a small Express 5 API using the native mongodb driver). Despite the geolocation name, there is no location code: no expo-location dependency, no geofencing, and the Location and Future/Location tab files (Location.jsx, FutureTab.jsx, LocationTab.jsx) are empty 0-byte files. The only working feature is a Today task list with status filters and status toggling. The README describes more than is built, such as PATCH updates and a tests suggestion, but no tests exist.

deepDive.title: Expo app shell and navigation
deepDive.body: toDo/app/_layout.tsx renders an expo-router Stack with headers hidden, and app/index.tsx composes the User profile component above the ToDo component inside a column View. Despite @react-navigation/bottom-tabs being installed, tabs are implemented by hand: ToDo.jsx keeps a currentMenu useState ('Locations', 'Today', 'Future') and renders a TouchableOpacity row with underline and bold styling for the active item. However the body always renders <TodayTab /> regardless of currentMenu, so the Locations and Future menus switch only the highlight, not the content.

deepDive.title: TodayTab: state, filters and data loading
deepDive.body: TodayTab.jsx initialises tasks state from the bundled tasks.json examples, then on mount calls fetchRuns() which does fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/runs') and replaces state only if the response is an array. Filtering uses a FILTERS constant (All, Open, Closed, WIP) and a filteredTasks(filter) helper that compares task.status case-insensitively, so each filter pill shows a live count. Tasks render in a ScrollView of Task components, keyed by tasks.indexOf(task). Because the URL is hard-coded to localhost, the app cannot reach the server from a physical phone, which matches the commit about ghost behavior on iPhone versus web.

deepDive.title: Task card and status cycling
deepDive.body: Task.jsx normalises missing fields by mutating the task prop: any of title, description, date, time, status, location that is falsy or the string 'null' becomes 'No <Attr>'. Status cycles Open -> WIP -> Closed -> Open through nextStatus, which calls the onStatusChange callback and then sets a local useState copy so the circle icon and strike or WIP styling update immediately. Long descriptions over 120 characters are truncated with an ellipsis and toggle open on press via an expanded flag. Mutating props and duplicating status in local state are shortcuts that can drift from the parent tasks array; also tasks.json uses lowercase 'open' while the component compares against 'Open'.

deepDive.title: Optimistic updates and the missing PATCH endpoint
deepDive.body: handleStatusChange in TodayTab updates local state immediately via setTasks with a map, then awaits updateTaskStatus(task.id, newStatus), which sends PATCH /api/runs/:id with JSON {status}. The server never implemented this route: server.js only defines GET /api/runs, so the PATCH returns 404, the error is logged with console.error, and the failure is not rolled back in the UI. In addition MongoDB documents carry _id rather than id, so task.id is likely undefined for real data. This is the exact bug the author chased in commit 0a91025 ('status not saving after app refresh') and it remains unsolved in the final code.

deepDive.title: Express server and MongoDB access pattern
deepDive.body: server/server.js requires dotenv, exits the process if MONGO_URI is not set, and creates a MongoClient with ServerApiVersion.v1 strict mode. The single route GET /api/runs calls client.connect(), reads db 'todo' collection 'todo_list' with find({}).toArray(), returns JSON or a 500 with err.message, and then closes the client in finally. Connecting and closing on every request, using one shared client object, is fragile: concurrent requests can close a connection another request is using. Commit 76b7b15 fixed the earlier 'immature closing' of the process by replacing a one-shot ping script with a long-lived Express listener. cors() and express.json() are applied globally with no auth.

deepDive.title: Stub controller files under server/api
deepDive.body: server/api holds locations.controller.js, tasks.controller.js, users.controller.js, runs.controller.js and a frontend/ folder with location, todo and user controllers. All but runs.controller.js are placeholder Express routers that return a 'not implemented' JSON message, and none of the controllers are mounted in server.js. runs.controller.js duplicates the server.js query but reads a 'runs' collection from the default DB in the URI and logs a MONGODB_URI message although it reads MONGO_URI. So there are two competing definitions of the runs endpoint and the real one is the inline route.

title: Schedule Short
description: An Expo app that imports a staff schedule CSV and parses it into per-person schedule objects.
overview: Users pick a CSV file with expo-document-picker. A custom parser walks the file line by line, detects the day-label row, the date row and role section headers (RN, CST, FA), and builds a Person object for each employee with their dated availability.
highlights: Hand-written CSV parser that identifies header, date and role-section rows by column content and a regex (d{1,2}-Mon)
Person class that stores a schedule keyed by date, with a date-to-weekday map
Role tracking: the current section (RN, CST, FA) is remembered and applied to each person row below it
getWeek(n) slices the date-keyed schedule into 7-day windows and throws on out-of-range weeks
demoDescription: Choose a CSV schedule file and the app parses it into structured people and dates.
demoBullets: Only CSV files are accepted
A Working indicator shows during processing
Parsed people and counts are logged to the console
Runs on web, iOS and Android through Expo

diagramSteps.detail: Each line is split on commas and checked for day-label, date and role rows.

systemDesign: The Expo app has a screen that calls a file-import component and then a pure parsing function in controller/organize.js, which returns an object of Person instances keyed by name. A small Express server folder also exists. The day.js and week.js controller files are empty placeholders.
learned: I learned to parse a messy, real-world spreadsheet export by detecting row types instead of assuming a clean format, and to model the result with a class. The parser is fragile: it splits on commas, so quoted fields would break it, and it relies on fixed column positions. The Person.changeRole method also references a field that does not exist, so I would clean that up and add tests.

deepDive.title: CSV parsing by row-shape detection
deepDive.body: schedule/controller/organize.js exports parseScheduleContent(fileContent), which splits the file on newlines and each line on commas, with no quoting support. Instead of assuming a fixed layout it classifies rows by shape: a row whose column 4 equals 'S' is the day-label header (dayIndex), and a row whose column 5 matches /^\d{1,2}-[A-Za-z]{3}$/ (and column 0 is not 'RN') is the date row (dates, sliced to drop the trailing column). Rows starting with RN, CST, FA or FAs set a running 'current' role, and any other non-empty, non-'Total' first column is treated as a person name. This makes the parser tolerant of section headers but tightly coupled to one specific spreadsheet export; any layout change breaks it silently.

deepDive.title: Two-pass merge of repeated names
deepDive.body: A person can appear on more than one row, so parseScheduleContent branches on data_.hasOwnProperty(name). The first occurrence builds a Person and records only 'D' or 'X' cells as shifts, writing null for every other column via addSchedule(date, null). A later row for the same name only fills dates that are still null (checkDate(date) === null) and only accepts 'B' or 'X'. The apparent intent is a day row followed by a second row for another shift type, but nothing in the code documents that, so it is inferred. A date of undefined can also be written as a key in the first branch when the column has no date, which Day.jsx later has to filter out.

deepDive.title: Person class and schedule storage
deepDive.body: Person holds name, pos (role), fte (hard-coded to 1), hour (taken from column 3), a schedule map of date string to lowercased code, and a dateDay map from date to weekday label. addSchedule is write-once per date, while changeSchedule overwrites. The date keys are strings like '14-Jul' with no year, so ordering depends on insertion order and on string sorting in the UI. changeRole is dead code that references this[day].role, which does not exist.

deepDive.title: Week slicing with getWeek
deepDive.body: Person.getWeek(weekInt) takes Object.keys(this.schedule), computes start = (weekInt-1)*7 and returns the next seven entries, padding missing slots with 'empty_N' keys. It throws 'Week index out of bounds' if the start is past the last key or if every value in the slice is null. This means weeks are defined by position in the key list rather than by calendar date, so a schedule that does not begin on the first column of a week would be sliced incorrectly. WeekCards.jsx wraps the call in try/catch and returns null for people with no shifts that week, which is how 'who is working this week' is derived without a separate query.

deepDive.title: Expo Router UI and view switching
deepDive.body: app/index.tsx holds parsedData and viewMode ('individual' | 'week' | 'day') in useState and renders one of Individual, Week or Day under a three-button menu. ImportFile.jsx uses expo-document-picker, rejects anything whose mimeType is not text/csv, and offers Reset and Submit. Submit passes the file URI to handleFileSubmit, which reads it with fetch(fileUri).then(r => r.text()), a pattern that works for local URIs in Expo but is not wrapped in error handling. The isProcessing flag is set to true and never reset, and the screen shows a literal 'Working' label even after parsing finishes.

deepDive.title: Day view and dropdown date selection
deepDive.body: Day.jsx collects every date key across all people into a Set, drops falsy and 'undefined' keys, and sorts with the default string sort. That sort is lexicographic, so '10-Jul' sorts before '9-Jul'; this is a real latent bug for date strings without zero padding. It then picks the first date by calling setSelectedDate during render, which is an anti-pattern in React but works here, and filters people whose schedule[selectedDate] is truthy. The dropdown is a plain TouchableOpacity plus ScrollView list. The arrow glyphs in the file are mojibake (encoding damage), visible in the source.

deepDive.title: Server scaffolding is non-functional
deepDive.body: server/server.js, added in the last feature commits, is a stub that is not valid JavaScript: it uses top-level await inside a non-async main(), and 'const {APISTRING} from .env' is a syntax error. It was meant to connect mongoose to MongoDB using a connection string from the environment, but handleError and logError are undefined, and the Expo app never calls it. server/package.json has only a start script. The parser and all views run entirely on-device, and nothing is persisted.

deepDive.title: Testing, empty files and debug leftovers
deepDive.body: There are no tests. controller/day.js and controller/week.js are zero-byte placeholders, and the Individual component still has console.log calls dumping the entire userInfo object on every render. The sample schedule.csv (real roster data) was committed once and later deleted and gitignored, so it is only in history; this is a privacy lesson worth stating plainly. The project is a working prototype for viewing a staff roster, not a finished product.

title: Authentication
description: Express and MongoDB authentication API with bcrypt password hashing and JWT token issuing, paired with a React client.
overview: A learning project that builds a username/password auth backend. The Express server mounts a router at /api/auth with register and login endpoints, stores users in MongoDB through a Mongoose schema, hashes passwords with bcrypt, and signs JSON Web Tokens with a secret from environment variables.
highlights: Registration salts and hashes passwords with bcrypt.genSalt(10) and bcrypt.hash before saving
Login returns a signed JWT built from the user id, with the secret read from process.env
Separate jwtHelper utility with generateToken (1 hour expiry) and verifyToken that returns null on failure
Mongoose schema enforces required, unique and trimmed usernames and has a verifyPassword method using bcrypt.compare
Generic 'Invalid username or password' message so login does not reveal which part was wrong
demoDescription: Register a user, then log in to receive a token the client can attach to later requests.
demoBullets: POST /api/auth/register creates a user with a hashed password
Duplicate usernames are rejected with a 400
POST /api/auth/login checks the password and returns a JWT
Configuration such as MONGODB_URI and JWT_SECRET comes from environment variables

diagramSteps.detail: React client posts username and password as JSON to /api/auth.

diagramSteps.title: Lookup
diagramSteps.detail: Mongoose queries the User collection by username.

diagramSteps.detail: Register hashes with a bcrypt salt; login compares against the stored hash.
