systemDesign: A three-folder repo (client, front, server). The server is an Express app with CORS and JSON middleware, a mounted auth router, a Mongoose User model, and a small JWT helper module. Secrets and the database URI are read from environment variables.
learned: I learned the basic shape of a token-based auth backend: salting and hashing passwords, never storing plaintext, and signing JWTs with an env secret. The code is still a work in progress. The login route calls bcrypt.password instead of bcrypt.compare, signs its token without an expiry (the helper has a 1 hour one but the route does not use it), and jwtHelper mixes ES imports with module.exports. Writing it showed me how easy those mistakes are, and that I need tests and a verify-token middleware to protect routes.

deepDive.title: Repository layout: three overlapping codebases
deepDive.body: The repo holds three directories: server/ (Express 5 + Mongoose API), client/ (an earlier Next.js attempt) and front/ (a second Next.js frontend added on 2025-04-09 in commit 5e43292). They were not consolidated, so there are two parallel client implementations and two different ways of talking to MongoDB. The README describes client/ and a server-mediated flow, while the later, more complete code lives in front/. There is no test suite; server/package.json still has the default 'echo Error: no test specified' test script.

deepDive.title: Mongoose user model and password verification
deepDive.body: server/models/user.js defines a Mongoose schema with username (String, required, unique, trim), password (String, required) and a tokens array of required strings. It attaches an instance method verifyPassword(password) that calls bcrypt.compare against the stored hash. The model is exported with ES module export default after commit a58ad57 converted it from module.exports. The tokens array is declared but never populated by any route, so it is scaffolding for refresh-token storage that was not built.

deepDive.title: Express routes: register and login
deepDive.body: server/routes/auth.js exposes POST /register and POST /login, mounted at /api/auth in server/server.js. Register checks User.findOne({username}) for duplicates, generates a salt with bcrypt.genSalt(10), hashes with bcrypt.hash, saves, and returns the new userId; failures are caught and return a 500 'Internal Server error'. Login uses a single generic 'Invalid username or password' message for both unknown user and bad password, which avoids user enumeration. However login calls bcrypt.password(...), which is not a bcrypt function (it should be bcrypt.compare), so this route would throw at runtime, and it has no try/catch. It also signs jwt.sign({userId}, JWT_SECRET) with no expiresIn even though the comment claims a 1 hour expiry.

deepDive.title: JWT helper that does not match the module system
deepDive.body: server/utils/jwtHelper.js defines generateToken (signs {id, email} with JWT_SECRET, expiresIn 1h) and verifyToken (jwt.verify with a callback, returning null on error). It loads secrets via dotenv.config(). The file mixes ES import syntax with module.exports = {...}, which fails under ESM, and the User schema has no email field. It is also never imported by routes/auth.js, so it is effectively dead code and no authenticated middleware or protected route exists on the server.

deepDive.title: Server bootstrap, CORS and module configuration
deepDive.body: server/server.js connects with mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGODB_URI) using the deprecated useNewUrlParser/useUnifiedTopology options, then applies cors() (wide open, no origin allow-list) and express.json(). It listens on process.env.PORT or 3000, which is also Next's default port, so both would collide locally. A commit series on 2025-04-04 (55691be, 80e4837, a58ad57) fought ESM vs CommonJS; the final package.json places "type": "module" inside the scripts object rather than at the top level, which is not a valid way to enable ESM. No .env values are committed in the current tree.

deepDive.title: front/: direct-to-MongoDB service layer in the browser bundle
deepDive.body: front/src/api/apiService.js uses the native mongodb MongoClient (ServerApiVersion.v1, strict) with bcryptjs and jsonwebtoken, exposing checkLogin(email, password) and registerUser(email, password). Each function connects, queries a collection 'users' in a placeholder database named yourDatabaseName, compares or hashes with bcryptjs (cost 10), signs a 1 hour JWT using process.env.JWT_SECRET, and closes the client in finally. RegistrationForm.tsx imports registerUser directly, which means database credentials and the JWT secret would be needed in client-side code; this is an architectural flaw and the code was never made to work end to end. Also connect() runs at import time and closes the client immediately.

deepDive.title: Frontend forms and auth state
deepDive.body: front/src/app/pages/LoginForm.tsx is a client component using useState and axios to POST {email, password} to /api/login, with axios.isAxiosError narrowing to show the server message (introduced in 4cc4b78 to replace an 'as any' cast). RegistrationForm.tsx collects username, email and password but only passes email and password to registerUser. front/src/api/Auth.js defines an AuthContext/AuthProvider that reads a token from localStorage and exposes loading, and Dashboard.js redirects to /login via react-router-dom Navigate, even though the app is Next.js, and imports a non-existent ./AuthContext file. No /api/login route exists in front/, so the login form has no working backend target.

deepDive.title: client/: AuthProvider with axios interceptor and stubbed API routes
deepDive.body: client/src/components/AuthProvider.jsx sketches a memory-held access token pattern: on mount it calls api.get('/api/me') to hydrate the token, then a useLayoutEffect registers an axios request interceptor that sets the Authorization header unless config._retry is set, ejecting it on cleanup. The file is incomplete: useEffect is imported twice, useState is not imported, and the AuthContext provider is never exported as default. client/src/api/helper.js stores the token in localStorage (saveAuthToken/getAuthToken/clearAuthToken), which conflicts with the in-memory design. The Next API routes login.ts, auth/login.ts and create-session.ts are commented out or return placeholder responses, and lib/session.ts's encrypt is just base64, which is encoding rather than encryption.

deepDive.title: Secrets handling and repo hygiene
deepDive.body: A server/.env containing only a PORT value was committed (28e079e) and then removed with stop tracking (64da586); the .gitignore was changed from './env' to '.env*' (546cb04) and then deleted entirely (04060fa) before later gitignore files were added. Another commit added node_modules to history (cbab484). No secret keys appear in the final tree, but the churn shows the ignore rules were not understood at first. The README lists features (refresh tokens, protected routes) that the code does not implement.

title: Login Page
description: React and Express registration and login app backed by MySQL, with bcrypt password hashing and an email existence check.
overview: A full-stack authentication demo. The Express server connects to a local MySQL database, creates the database and a user table if they are missing, and exposes routes for adding, reading, updating and deleting users plus a login route that compares a submitted password against a stored bcrypt hash. The React client provides the registration and login forms with validation.
highlights: Passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds) before insertion into MySQL
Server bootstraps itself: falls back to creating the testServer database and a user table with a UNIQUE email column
Login route fetches the user by email and uses bcrypt.compare on the stored hash
/checkEmail endpoint returns { exists } so the client can validate an email before registering
README describes password validation and email checking on the React side

demoBullets: Registration form validates the password and checks whether the email already exists
New passwords are stored only as bcrypt hashes
Login responds with success, incorrect password, or not found
Requires a local MySQL server and the Express server running

systemDesign: A two-folder monolith: a client React app and a single server.js Express file. The server owns a single MySQL connection and creates its schema on startup. Everything is on localhost with hard-coded connection settings.
learned: I learned how a full-stack login fits together and how bcrypt hashing works with a SQL database. Honestly, the server is a learning prototype: many routes are GET requests that mutate data, and queries are built by string interpolation, which is open to SQL injection. Login also returns plain text and no session or token. If I revisit it I would use parameterized queries, POST/DELETE verbs, and issue a token or session.

deepDive.title: Two-tier layout: CRA client and Express server
deepDive.body: The repo is split into client/ (create-react-app, React 18, axios) and server/ (Express 4 with the mysql driver, bcrypt, cors and body-parser). The server listens on port 4000 and the client hard-codes http://localhost:4000 URLs in Login.jsx and Register.jsx. There is no environment config, proxy or production build wiring, so it only works as a local dev setup. dotenv and nodemailer are listed in server/package.json but are not used by server.js.

deepDive.title: Card component toggling Sign In and Register
deepDive.body: App.jsx renders a single Card component. Card keeps a formType state ('login' or 'register') and swaps between Login and Register, with one button whose label flips between 'Not a member? Sign Up' and 'Already a member? Sign In'. There is no router even though react-router-dom is installed, so the view is purely state-driven. Styling lives in CSS modules (Card.module.css, Login.module.css, Register.module.css); Card.module.css gives a centered 50%-wide panel with a box shadow.

deepDive.title: Client-side registration validation
deepDive.body: Register.handleSubmit runs checks in order: password equals confirmPassword, isPasswordValid(password), then an existence check via GET /checkEmail/:email. isPasswordValid in utils/PasswordValidation.jsx uses four regexes (uppercase, lowercase, digit, non-word special character) and fires a separate alert() on the first failure. The error text in Register.jsx ('one uppercase letter and one other character') no longer matches the stricter four-rule validator. EmailValidation.jsx and LoginValidation.jsx are stubs: the first is an empty function with a comment, the second only console.logs.

deepDive.title: Password hashing on the server
deepDive.body: Passwords are hashed with bcrypt (saltRounds = 10) before insert, in the /addpost route and in /updatepassword. The user table is (id AUTO_INCREMENT, email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE, password VARCHAR(255)). POST /login looks up the row by email, then calls bcrypt.compare and replies with plain text strings ('Incorrect password', 'Email not found', or a success message). It issues no session, cookie or JWT, so a successful login proves nothing afterwards.

deepDive.title: Security problems that remain
deepDive.body: The README describes a REST API (POST /register, PUT/DELETE /users/:id) secured with parameterized queries, but server.js does not match that: registration is GET /addpost/:email/:password, which puts the plaintext password in the URL and in server logs. Several routes build SQL by string interpolation (/getpost, /updateemail, /deletepost/:type/:id, /checkEmail, /login), which is SQL-injectable, and /droptable/:table and /confirmdbdelete are unauthenticated destructive GET endpoints. Only the /addpost insert uses a parameterized 'INSERT ... SET ?'. The MySQL connection uses root with an empty password on localhost. This is a learning project and should not be treated as production-safe.

deepDive.title: Database bootstrap and error handling
deepDive.body: server.js connects to a MySQL database named testServer; on a connection error it creates the database and the user table from inside the same callback. Many handlers use 'if (err) throw err' inside async callbacks, which crashes the process on a bad query. The login handler logs a database error but then still reads results.length, which would throw if results is undefined. The Register client also has a stray extra brace in the add-user URL template (${password}}) so the password sent to the server appears to include a trailing '}', which would be hashed in and make later logins fail for the true password.

deepDive.title: Unfinished client state
deepDive.body: bd11a22 added utils/UserProvider.jsx with a UserContext and setUser, and Login.jsx also defines its own UserContext and UserProvider and calls setUser(response.data.user). The server's login route sends a plain string, not a { user } object, and App.jsx never wraps the tree in a provider, so useContext would return undefined and destructuring setUser would throw on submit. client/userServer/userServer.js is empty and App.css is empty. The login flow therefore ends in a console.log or an error rather than any logged-in view.

architecture.summary: A React single-page client posts credentials to an Express API, which hashes passwords with bcrypt and stores users in a local MySQL database.

title: ToDo (React Native Task Tracker)
description: An Expo / React Native to-do app with status counters and tasks persisted on-device with AsyncStorage.
overview: ToDo is a React Native app built with Expo. Tasks are instances of a small Task class (text, date, type, tags, description) held in React state and serialized to AsyncStorage as JSON. A header row shows live counters for Complete, ToDo, Progress and Wait. A simpler sibling repo, ToDoIOS, is a minimal version of the same idea that keeps tasks in memory and tracks completion in a map keyed by task text.
highlights: Persists the task list as JSON in AsyncStorage and rehydrates it into Task objects on startup
Status counters (Complete, ToDo, Progress, Wait) built from an object map and memoized with useMemo
Add flow with input validation and a collapsible menu component
ToDoIOS variant: FlatList rendering, tap-to-strike-through, and a two-press confirm for Remove All
demoDescription: Add a task, see the counters update, and reopen the app to confirm tasks are still there.
demoBullets: Tap Add Task to open the input menu
Empty input is rejected with an alert
Tasks are saved to AsyncStorage after each add
Status chips show a count per category

systemDesign: A single screen component owns all state and passes setters down to child components (Menu, TaskBox). Storage is the only persistence layer, with no backend. Because JSON drops class methods and Dates become strings, loading re-wraps each record in the Task class.
learned: I learned that JSON serialization loses class methods and turns Dates into strings, so I had to rebuild Task instances when loading from AsyncStorage. I also learned the code works but has rough edges: the component holds many state variables and logs a lot, and my ToDoIOS version keys completion by task text, which breaks with duplicate tasks. Next time I would use ids.

deepDive.title: Two apps, one lineage
deepDive.body: ToDoIOS (Sept 2024, 4 commits) is a single-file Expo app: App.js keeps task, tasks (array of strings), a completedTasks map keyed by task text and a warning flag in useState, with FlatList rendering, a close.png remove button and tap to cross out. It is in-memory only, so everything is lost on restart. The later ToDo project (Oct 2024, 23 commits) is a rewrite named 'helper' in package.json, split into App.js, components/todo.js and assets/{Menu,TaskBox,task}.js, with AsyncStorage persistence, descriptions, types and tags. The two share no commit history; ToDo is a fresh repo, not a continuation of git history.

deepDive.title: Task model and date formatting
deepDive.body: assets/task.js exports a Task class with task, date, type (default 'Progress'), tags (default ['+']) and description, and accessor methods (showTask, showDate, showAllTags and so on). showDate formats with toLocaleDateString('en-US', {day, month:'long', year}) and builds a 12-hour clock string by hand: hours % 12 || 12 for midnight and noon, zero-padded minutes, and an AM/PM period. The sentinel '+' tag is a UI trick: it marks the add-tag button slot inside the tags array instead of being separate state. Class instances are lost on JSON round trip, so loading has to rebuild them.

deepDive.title: Persistence with AsyncStorage
deepDive.body: components/todo.js loads on mount with loadTasks(): AsyncStorage.getItem('tasks'), JSON.parse, then map to new Task(task.task, new Date(task.date), type, tags, description) so dates are revived and methods restored. saveTasks stringifies the array under the single 'tasks' key and logs the payload. Storage writes are scattered: todo.js's saveTasks, TaskBox's updateLocalStorage in a useEffect on [tasks], and direct setItem calls in updateTaskType, deleteTask and updateTasksWithNewTags. This means every TaskBox mounted writes the whole list whenever tasks changes, so N tasks cause N redundant writes per change.

deepDive.title: Tags and gesture detection in TaskBox
deepDive.body: TaskBox.jsx renders a horizontal FlatList of tag bubbles plus a trailing '+' button that swaps for a TextInput. addTag strips all whitespace with replace(/\s+/g, '') (making the later includes(' ') check dead) and removes the '+' placeholder before appending. A tag is deleted by a double press implemented by hand: handleTagPress stores {tag, time} in lastPressed and treats a second press on the same tag under 300 ms as a delete, falling back to ['+'] when no tags remain. Tag edits are copied back into the parent array by identity (task === taskText) and saved.

deepDive.title: Status types and the top filter bar
deepDive.body: Each task has a type among ToDo, Progress, Wait, Complete, changed through a per-task menu (updateTaskType). The top nav in todo.js builds navItem counts and memoizes navItemArray with useMemo, but the completed, toDo, progress and wait arrays that feed the counts are never populated (their setters are never called), so the badges stay at 0. selectedItem is stored for highlighting but not used to filter the list. A TODO at the top of TaskBox says changing type should update the nav lists, which confirms this is unfinished.

deepDive.title: Add-task flow and duplicated logic
deepDive.body: Menu.js and todo.js each contain nearly identical addTask functions: trim check, new Task(input, new Date(), 'ToDo', [], description), spread into a new array, setTasks and saveTasks, clear inputs, or alert('Must add task'). Only Menu's version is wired to the button; todo.js's copy is passed as a prop and ignored. In ToDoIOS, handlePress has a control-flow bug: the empty-task alert is a separate if from the length check, so an empty string still falls into the else and is added.

deepDive.title: Rough edges and hygiene
deepDive.body: Many console.log calls remain, including dumping all stored tasks after every save. FlatList keyExtractor uses index, and the FlatList is given a key prop in renderItem rather than the list, so deleting rows can rebind state (tags, menu) to the wrong item. The ToDo repo also tracks an accidental Windows file path (%ProgramData%/Microsoft/Windows/UUS/State/_active.uusver) from the 'added' commit 923bccf, and ToDoIOS committed a 15,000-line package-lock.json, then deleted the .gitignore. There are no tests for either app.

architecture.summary: On-device React Native (Expo) apps. ToDo keeps task objects in React state and mirrors the whole array to AsyncStorage; ToDoIOS is an earlier in-memory-only version.

title: toDoGeo (Task Countdown App)
description: An Expo Router TypeScript client with a task model that computes a live time-remaining countdown, plus a stub server folder.
overview: toDoGeo is an early-stage Expo Router app with a client and server folder. The working part is the ToDo component and a Task class that stores title, description, due date and completion, and computes a days/hours/minutes/seconds string from the due date. A one-second interval re-renders the list, and the remaining time is color-styled by urgency. The Locations component is only a stub, so no geofencing or distance math exists in the code yet.
highlights: Task class computes a days/hr/min/sec countdown with floor and modulo math on millisecond differences
setInterval tick re-renders the list every second, with cleanup on unmount
Urgency styling: more than 3 days, more than 1 day, or less than 1 day
Includes a Jest test file for the Task class
demoDescription: Seeded tasks show live ticking countdowns that change color as the due date approaches.
demoBullets: Toggle a task complete with a Switch
Clear completed removes finished tasks
Countdown updates every second
Color changes at 3-day and 1-day thresholds

diagramSteps.detail: Task holds title, description, due Date and completed flag.

diagramSteps.detail: useEffect sets a 1s interval that copies the task array to force a re-render.

The server folder only contains a package.json, and the Locations component is a placeholder for the intended location feature.
learned: I learned how to turn a millisecond difference into days, hours, minutes and seconds with floor and modulo, and how to run a timer safely in a React effect. Being honest about the state of the repo: the location-based part is not implemented yet, the data is hardcoded, and the Clear completed handler mutates state directly, which I left as a TODO to refactor.

deepDive.title: Task model and time-remaining math
deepDive.body: client/components/ToDo/task.js defines a Task class with title, description, a Date, and completed (default false), plus completeTask, getDate, getTask and getDescription. getTimeRemainingString() computes this.date - Date.now() and decomposes the millisecond difference with Math.floor and modulo chains (days from 86,400,000, hours from the remainder mod a day, minutes mod an hour, seconds mod a minute) into '3 days, 4 hr, 2 m, 45 s'. It does not clamp negative values, so an overdue task shows negative days and a floor of a negative remainder, which gives odd values. The earlier design had a separate time parameter; 7f79466 removed it because the Date already carries the time.

deepDive.title: Live countdown rendering
deepDive.body: ToDo.jsx seeds five hard-coded Task objects with dates offset from Date.now() (about 1 day, 3 days and 4 days out). A useEffect sets a setInterval(1000) that calls setTasks([...currentTasks]) to force a re-render each second, so the countdown strings recompute in render. The effect depends on currentTasks and therefore re-creates the interval whenever the array changes, which is wasteful but functional. getTimeRemainingStyle picks one of timeRemainingHigh (>3 days), Medium (>1 day) or Low style in ToDoStyles.js, which gives the red/amber/green style urgency coloring.

deepDive.title: Completion toggle and Clear completed
deepDive.body: toggleTaskCompletion(index) copies the array and mutates the task's completed flag, then calls setTasks, driven by a React Native Switch per row. The 'Clear completed' button in 72e3362 splices completed tasks out of currentTasks in place inside the onPress handler but never calls setTasks, so the removal only becomes visible when the one-second interval re-renders; a TODO comment in the file admits it should move into a Tasks class. Because it mutates state directly it is a bug-prone approach rather than an idiomatic update.

deepDive.title: Unit tests with Jest
deepDive.body: task.test.js uses the jest-expo preset (npm test runs jest --watchAll). Tests cover construction defaults, completeTask, a 1-hour future date, and the time string using a Date built from 3 days + 4 hr + 2 min + 45 s. Two tests are out of sync with the code: one calls task.getTimeRemaining(), which was never implemented, and the toString test expects a string without the time field while the class's toString still concatenates this.time (undefined) and the expectation hard-codes a UTC timezone string. The time-string test is also timing-sensitive, since seconds can tick over between construction and call. So the suite as committed would not be fully green.

deepDive.title: App shell and placeholders
deepDive.body: client/app/index.tsx (Expo Router) renders a User header and the ToDo list in a column. User.jsx is a mock header with via.placeholder.com images, 'Good Morning / Username' text and two menu images whose onTouchEnd only console.log, with brightly colored debug backgrounds. Locations.jsx, which would hold the location-based part implied by the name toDoGeo, is just a text stub. The geo feature is not implemented; no location APIs are used.

deepDive.body: Expo auto-generated files were committed and deleted in alternation (3459d00 deleted app.json; 63d7ade says 'autogenerated new settings on run' for .expo). The final commit 2da35a7 commented out the extends line in client/tsconfig.json, which is invalid JSON syntax tolerated by tsc, as a 'temp solution' to silence an error. The backend (e9e2e18) is only a server/package.json with no server code, and the README is a single heading.

description: A React web app scaffold paired with an Express and MySQL REST API for storing notes.
overview: my-life is a Create React App front end (App, Main and Nav components) with a Node/Express server that connects to a local MySQL database, creates the 'notes' database and table if missing, and exposes endpoints to add, fetch, list and delete notes. It is an early prototype: the sibling repos noteDiary and CalenderDiary are near-empty scaffolds, so they are not documented separately.
highlights: Express REST API with add, get, delete and list-all note routes
Self-bootstrapping schema: creates the database and notes table if absent
Table uses auto-increment id and a default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP date_created column
Insert uses mysql's parameterized SET ? form

GET /getallnotes returns all rows as JSON

systemDesign: A two-tier setup: a CRA front end and a single-file Express server on port 4000 using callback-style mysql queries. The schema is created at startup, so no migration step is needed locally. The database connects as root with an empty password, which is only suitable for local development.
learned: I learned how to wire an Express server to MySQL and bootstrap a schema at startup. Looking back honestly, the code has flaws: the get and delete routes build SQL by string interpolation, which is open to SQL injection, errors are only logged so the response can still crash, and getnote does not return the row. I would use parameterized queries and proper error handling next time.

deepDive.title: Calendar grid generation in Calender.js
deepDive.body: my-life/src/assets/Calender.js defines a Calender class with a months table mapping 1-12 to [name, dayCount]. February's length comes from this.leapYear = year % 4 === 0, which is wrong for century years such as 2100 (a simplification, not a full Gregorian rule). calendarToList(setMonth) finds the weekday of the 1st with new Date(year, setMonth - 1, 1).getDay() and builds an array of week arrays, headed by ['Su','M ','T ','W ','Th','F ','Sa']. Leading blank cells are three-space strings only on the first week, and days are padStart(2,' ') strings. The earlier createCalender() produced an ASCII table with the same math and is still in the file as a leftover.

deepDive.title: React month navigation
deepDive.body: Calender.jsx keeps currentMonth (initialised from new Date().getMonth() + 1) and a calendarOutput array in state; a useEffect keyed on currentMonth instantiates the class and calls calendarToList. goBack and goForward clamp to 1..12 and the buttons get a CSS 'hidden' class at the bounds, so the calendar cannot roll across a year. The month label uses new Date(2024, currentMonth - 1).toLocaleString('default', {month:'long'}) with the year hard-coded to 2024, while the class itself uses the current year, an inconsistency. Each week is mapped to Day components that just print the string.

deepDive.title: Date and note model
deepDive.body: assets/Date.js defines a Dates class intended to hold notes per date: notes is an object of date -> array of {id, note}, with an auto-incrementing nextNoteId, addNote, deleteNote (findIndex then splice) and getNote. It also has helpers returning zero-padded month, day and year strings, and getCurrentDate overwrites this.today with a 'mm/dd/yyyy' string, which would break later calls. Dates.js is not imported by any component after the calendar refactor (the require was removed in 9f6c09c), so notes never reach the UI. The Item.js file is a one-field placeholder class.

deepDive.title: Express and MySQL notes API
deepDive.body: my-life/server/server.js is an Express app on port 4000 with cors and body-parser. It connects to a local MySQL database called 'notes' as root with an empty password, falling back to connecting without a database and running CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS, then CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes(id, note TEXT, date_created TIMESTAMP, subject VARCHAR(255)). Routes are POST /addnote, GET /getnote/:id, DELETE /deletenote/:id and GET /getallnotes. The id routes interpolate req.params.id straight into SQL strings, which is injectable, and the error handling only console.logs then dereferences result, which would throw on a failed query. GET /getnote/:id answers with a status string instead of the row.

deepDive.title: Sidebar and UI scaffolding
deepDive.body: SideNav.jsx declares state for upcoming, today, search, tags, list and a calenderToggle, but nothing populates them. The counts render `upcoming ? 0 : upcoming.length`, an inverted ternary that always shows 0 for a truthy object and would crash for null; the comments in the file list the intended Upcoming, Today, Lists and Tags features. It also imports toFormData from axios without using it. Unit.jsx truncates its content prop to 4 characters via useEffect, and Unit-ChatGPT.jsx is a near-duplicate kept in the tree.

deepDive.title: Unwired components and broken imports
deepDive.body: Note, NoteList, NoteCard, NoteShow, Timer, CountDown and TopNav are stubs. Note.jsx imports '/Note.module.css' with an absolute path, NoteCard and NoteShow take positional arguments instead of a props object (so title would receive the props object), and NoteList treats its props object as noteCount. None of these are mounted: App.jsx renders only SideNav and Calender. The app shell is index.jsx with React.StrictMode.

deepDive.title: Testing and state of completion
deepDive.body: There are no tests. The project got as far as a navigable month grid in the React client and a standalone CRUD server; notes, timer and todo features are comments and empty components.

title: Fitness Site
description: A multi-page fitness website built with plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, featuring muscle group pages, a video carousel, dark mode and form validation.
overview: Fitness Site is a static front-end project with no framework or build step. It has a main fitness.html page, a catalog page, per-muscle-group pages, and a single script.js that handles section switching, a vertical video carousel, a dark mode toggle and contact form validation.
highlights: Class-based section switching with a toggleDisplay helper that hides the current section and shows the next
Vertical video carousel that rotates items by moving DOM nodes with insertBefore and appendChild
Dark mode implemented by toggling a single dark-mode class on the body from a checkbox
Contact form validation with required-field checks and a regular expression for email format
demoDescription: A tour of the single-page navigation, muscle group video carousel and theme toggle.
demoBullets: Switch between sections without a page reload
Scroll through exercise videos with up and down controls
Toggle dark mode with one checkbox
Submit the contact form and see validation messages

systemDesign: A static multi-page site served directly from files. Layout and theme live in CSS (styles.css, catalog_style.css), behavior lives in one script.js, and muscle group content is split into separate pages under the musclegroups folder. State is kept in the DOM and one global variable, with no backend.
learned: This project taught me how far plain DOM APIs can go without a framework. Looking back, the navigation code has rough edges: currentClass starts as an HTMLCollection rather than a string, and the carousel registers two click handlers on the up button that overlap. I would clean those up, and a component framework would make the state handling simpler.

deepDive.title: Single-page shell driven by toggleDisplay
deepDive.body: fitness.html is a 44 KB page holding many top-level blocks (.home, .nutrition, .catalog, .muscle-group, .join). The nav links call toggleDisplay('workout'), toggleDisplay('nutrition') and so on from script.js, which hides the previously shown class and shows the new one with display:block. The tracking variable currentClass starts as an HTMLCollection (getElementsByClassName('home')) and is later replaced with a string, so the first call passes a collection into getElementsByClassName, which coerces it and likely hides nothing. This is a simple show/hide router with no history or URL state.

deepDive.title: Dark mode via a body class
deepDive.body: A checkbox with id darkMode in the nav has a change listener that calls document.body.classList.toggle('dark-mode', event.target.checked). All theming is done by styles.css rules under body.dark-mode, with no persistence in localStorage, so the choice resets on reload. The listener is attached at script load time with getElementById, so script.js is only safe on pages that contain that checkbox; catalog.html loads the same script.js but has no darkMode element or carousel, which would throw TypeErrors there.

deepDive.title: Video carousel logic
deepDive.body: The muscle-group section has a .carousel of .video-item elements with up and down buttons. Down moves the first item to the end via appendChild; up inserts the last item before the first. A separate updateCarousel() applies translateY(-itemHeight * currentItem) but is only called from a first up-click handler that decrements a counter. So two competing mechanisms (DOM rotation and CSS translate) are mixed, and the transform path rarely does anything meaningful. The carousel is rotated by reordering nodes, which is effectively a circular queue.

deepDive.title: Join form validation
deepDive.body: The join form (#joinForm) calls validateForm() on submit, which reads fields via document.forms['myForm'] while the form's actual id is joinForm. If the form has no name attribute of myForm, that lookup returns undefined and throws. When it works, it checks name and email are non-empty and tests the email against /^[\w-]+(\.[\w-]+)*@([\w-]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,7}$/. The form action is '#' with method POST, so nothing is ever sent; there is no backend.

deepDive.title: Exercise catalog and muscle-group pages
deepDive.body: catalog.html lists links grouped Upper Body (back, bicep, chest, shoulders, tricep), Lower Body (quads, hamstrings, calfs) and Core (abs) into musclegroups/*.html. Each page is hand-written HTML with an h2 exercise name, a description paragraph and an ordered list of steps, styled by musclegroups/exercises_style.css. Pages duplicate the nav and copy images (logo.png, abs.jpg) into the folder. Some nav links in those pages point to files that do not exist (home.html, workout_routines.html, stories.html, nutrition.html), and shoulders/tricep have no matching image names consistently.

deepDive.title: Layout and assets
deepDive.body: styles.css (about 14 KB) uses CSS grid for .content-grid (repeat() columns with a 20px gap), flexbox for the nav and muscle sections (a 70% muscle area plus a 25% video column), and transition effects on hover (box-shadow, transform 0.5s). A parallax background is used on the join section. The images folder holds multi-megabyte files (banner.jpg about 4.9 MB, bench.jpeg about 6 MB) and a 37 MB workoutDemoVid.mp4 committed directly in git with autoplay and muted on the video element, so the repo is heavy and pages load slowly. Several sections in fitness.html carry the comment 'class not in use', which shows leftover markup.

title: React Spotify Playlist App (Work in Progress)
description: An in-progress React playlist builder with a client split into SearchBar, SearchResults, Playlist, Tracklist and Track components, plus an Express and MySQL server scaffold.
overview: This repo has a client/server layout. The React client defines a component tree for searching tracks and building a playlist, with App holding the state. The Spotify API module and several App handlers are still stubs, and the Express server currently only sets up middleware and a MySQL connection.

App owns search results, playlist name and playlist tracks in useState and passes handlers down
Handlers wrapped in useCallback, with addTracks skipping tracks already in the playlist by id
Express server scaffold with cors, body-parser and a MySQL connection, with bcrypt required for later auth work

learned: I practiced lifting state up and structuring components around single responsibilities. The project is honestly unfinished: removeTrack, updatePlaylist and savePlaylist are empty stubs, the Spotify module has no API calls, and the server has no routes. Finishing it would mean implementing the OAuth flow and those handlers.

deepDive.title: Project scope: a Jammming-style playlist builder, unfinished
deepDive.body: The README describes a React app where you search Spotify, add tracks to a playlist, rename it and save it to your account. In the code, only the component scaffolding and part of the state logic exist. client/src/components/util/spotify.js is a one-line comment ('This file will be in charge of connecting to Spotify API'), so there is no OAuth flow, no token handling and no fetch call to the Spotify Web API. The README therefore describes intended behavior rather than what the code does today.

deepDive.title: Component tree and prop flow
deepDive.body: The tree is App -> SearchBar, SearchResults -> Tracklist -> Track, and Playlist -> Tracklist -> Track. SearchBar keeps the term in local useState and calls props.onSearch(term) via useCallback. Tracklist maps tracks to Track elements keyed by track.id and forwards onAdd, onRemove and isRemoval. Track renders a '+' or '-' button depending on isRemoval, which lets one component serve both the results list and the playlist.

deepDive.title: App state and callbacks
deepDive.body: App holds three states: searchResult, playlistName ('New Playlist') and playlistTracks. search calls Spotify.search(term).then(setSearchResult), but Spotify has no default export in spotify.js, so that call would fail. addTracks is the only finished handler: it ignores duplicates with playlistTracks.some(t => t.id === track.id) and otherwise appends using the functional setState form. removeTrack, updatePlaylist and savePlaylist are empty useCallback bodies, and App's return is a bare <div> with a comment saying the HTML still needs to be set up, so nothing renders.

deepDive.title: Bugs in the component files
deepDive.body: Tracklist.jsx uses the attribute classname (lowercase) instead of className and imports '/Tracklist.module.css' with an absolute path that will not resolve. SearchResults.jsx imports '/SearchResults.jsx', which is itself, and App imports Tracklist without using it. Track.jsx imports './Track.css' but the file in the folder is Track.module.css, and every .module.css file is empty (0 bytes), so there is no styling at all. The CSS module files are also imported as plain side-effect imports, so they would not provide scoped class names anyway.

deepDive.title: Server stub
deepDive.body: server/server.js sets up Express with cors and body-parser JSON, and creates a MySQL connection to a database named spotify as root with an empty password on localhost. It requires bcrypt but never uses it, declares no routes and never calls app.listen, so it does nothing when started. It is boilerplate copied from the author's login-page project, and the comment at the top still talks about connecting to the Spotify API.

deepDive.title: Repository history reflects a one-day build
deepDive.body: All twelve commits fall on 2024-07-22 and 2024-07-23. The work went in top-down: static components, search bar, playlist creation, search results, add/remove tracks, then the util file. A file was added as util/server.js, deleted, and re-added as util/spotify.js across three commits, and the final feature commit (5a1017b) lists useStates and functions that are mostly empty. The project stopped before the Spotify integration or any UI composition was finished.
